content: The incubation period, also referred to as the latent period or latency period, is the duration of time that passes between exposure to a pathogenic organism, chemical, or radiation and the initial appearance of symptoms and signs of the disease. This period can range from as short as a few minutes to as long as 30 years, as observed in the case of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Although the terms latent period and incubation period are sometimes used interchangeably, a distinction is occasionally made. The incubation period specifically refers to the time between infection and the clinical onset of the disease, whereas the latent period refers to the time from infection to the point at which the individual becomes infectious. The relative length of these periods depends on the specific disease in question. An individual may carry a disease, such as Streptococcus in the throat, without displaying any symptoms. Depending on the disease, the person may or may not be capable of transmitting the disease to others during the incubation period. Examples of Incubation Periods Incubation periods can vary significantly and are typically expressed as a range. When possible, it is ideal to report the mean incubation period along with the 10th and 90th percentiles, although such detailed data is not always available. The values for incubation periods are often presented in ascending order based on the number of days, though in some cases, the mean value must be inferred. For many diseases, the incubation period tends to be longer in adults compared to children or infants.
